summary: This RFC introduces domain-style names, how they serve ARPA Internet mail and host addresses, and the protocol and servers that implement them. It is an early concept document for the Domain Name System. It was replaced by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo set out the ideas behind domain names: one tree of names, split across many servers so no single machine holds everything, and a small program on each host that turns a name into an address by asking those servers.

questions: how did the original domain name system work
what is a zone of authority
subtitle: The 1983 concept paper that proposed replacing one central host table with a distributed, tree-shaped database of domain names.

tldr.problem: Hosts were listed in one global table kept by the Network Information Center, and that table was near the limit of manageability. Mailbox names had grown into an irregular set of ad hoc formats that each user had to understand.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes a tree-structured name space held in a distributed database. Name servers are authoritative for pieces of that tree, called zones, and resolvers query name servers on behalf of user programs, following referrals when a server is not authoritative.
tldr.outcome: RFC 882 is a concept memo. It was superseded by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 and updated by RFC 973.

today: RFC 882 is a 1983 concept memo for the domain name system, and it has been superseded: RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 took over the job of specifying the domain system, and RFC 973 updated this memo.

sections.title: Why Domain Names Were Needed
sections.content:
The memo opens with the problem. As applications grow to span multiple hosts, then networks, and finally internets, they also span multiple administrative boundaries and different methods of operation. The number of resources, such as mailboxes, and the number of locations for those resources make it hard to create consistent ways of referring to resources that are similar but scattered across the environment.

The ARPA Internet illustrates the size problem. There had to be a mapping between host names such as USC-ISIF and ARPA Internet addresses such as 10.2.0.52, and the mechanism in use was a global table kept by the Network Information Center and published as the file HOSTS.TXT. The size of that table, and especially the frequency of updates to it, were near the limit of manageability. What was needed was a distributed database that performs the same function.

The mail problem was worse. Mail system implementers had long ago recognised the impossibility of centralising mailbox names, and had created an increasingly large and irregular set of methods for identifying where a mailbox was. Some involved routes and forwarding hosts as part of the mail destination address, which forced users to know several address formats and the capabilities of various forwarders.
sections.plainLanguage: One shared list of every host in the Internet was getting too big to keep up to date, and mail addresses had turned into a patchwork of formats nobody could simplify. The memo argues for names that live in a database spread across many machines.

sections.title: The Three Parts of the Domain System
sections.content:
The proposed solution has three major components.

The domain name space is a tree-structured name space. Conceptually, each node and leaf of the tree names a set of information, and query operations extract specific types of information from a particular set. A query names the domain name of interest and describes the type of resource information desired. Domain names are not required to have a one-to-one correspondence with host names, host addresses, or any other type of information.

Name servers are server programs holding information about the domain tree's structure and its sets of information. A name server may cache information about any part of the tree, but in general a particular name server has complete information about a subset of the domain space and pointers to other name servers. The parts for which a name server has complete information are called zones, and the name server is an authority for them.

Resolvers are programs that extract information from name servers in response to user requests. A resolver must be able to access at least one name server and use that server's information to answer a query directly, or pursue the query using referrals to other name servers. A resolver is typically a system routine directly accessible to user programs, so no protocol is needed between the resolver and the user program.
sections.plainLanguage: The design has three moving parts: a tree of names, the servers that hold pieces of that tree, and the local library that user programs call to look things up.

sections.title: The Name Space and Resource Records
sections.content:
The domain name space is a tree structure. Each node and leaf on the tree corresponds to a resource set, which may be empty, and each has an associated label. Labels are not guaranteed to be unique, except for the root node, which has a null label. The domain name of a node is the path from the root to that node, and by convention the labels are read left to right, from the most specific to the least specific. Internally, programs represent domain names as sequences of labels, where each label is a length octet followed by an octet string, and a length byte of zero terminates the name. Printed domain names separate labels with dots.

To simplify implementations, the total number of octets representing label octets and label lengths is limited to 255, so a printed domain name can be up to 254 characters. A special label, the asterisk, matches any other single label, so *.ARPA matches FOO.ARPA but not FOO.BAR.ARPA.

A domain name identifies a set of resource information, composed of separate resource records. Each record has an owner name, management information such as length fields and timeouts, a resource type field that is two octets long, a class field that identifies the format of the resource data and is also two octets long, and the resource data itself. The resource data always starts with a two octet length field, which lets a name server or resolver find the boundaries of the data even if it cannot understand it.
sections.plainLanguage: Names are stored as a tree of labels, and each label holds a set of records. A record says what kind of thing it is, which format the data uses, and the data itself.

sections.title: How a Name Server Answers a Query
sections.content:
A query to a name server must include a domain name identifying the target resource set, called QNAME, and the type and class of the desired records, called QTYPE and QCLASS. Both may hold special values that match more than one type or class: the QTYPE field may hold MAILA, which matches all mail agent records, or an asterisk, which matches any record type; the QCLASS field may hold an asterisk, which matches any class. Because a name server may not know all of the classes in the system, it can never know whether it is authoritative for all of them, so responses to QCLASS=* queries can never be authoritative.

When a name server is asked about a name it is authoritative for, it returns the resource information or an indication that the name does not exist. When it is asked about a name outside its authority, it returns the information it has and also a response pointing toward an authoritative name server. If a name server is not an authority for a query, it can never return a negative response.

The memo gives pseudocode for the processing. The server walks up the containing domains of QNAME, starting at the root. If it meets an SOA record it knows it is authoritative, unless it finds a lower NS record that delegates authority. If it is not authoritative, it copies the NS records for the closest delegation into the response. Finally it copies all records that match the query into the response. A separate rule applies to the CNAME record: when a name server fails to find a requested record for a name, it checks whether the resource set contains a CNAME record with a matching class, and if so includes it and continues the query at the domain name in the CNAME's data field.
sections.plainLanguage: When a server is asked about a name it owns, it answers. When it is asked about a name above or below its part of the tree, it points the asker at the server that does own it.

sections.title: Resolvers, Caching and Timeouts
sections.content:
Two general approaches exist for a distributed database when a query can only be answered by another server. The recursive approach has the first server pursue the query on the client's behalf. The iterative approach has the server refer the client to another server and let the client pursue the query. Both have advantages and disadvantages, but the iterative approach is preferred for datagram-style access, and the domain system requires it while allowing the recursive approach as an option.

A resolver must be able to chain through multiple name servers to reach an authoritative one. It should guard against loops in referrals, and a simple policy is to discard referrals that do not match more of the query name than the referring name server. It must also be able to try alternate name servers when one does not respond, and it must be able to report different failure conditions to its client: an unknown domain name, an unknown resource for a known name, and inability to reach any authoritative server.

Caching improves performance but is also a potential source of incorrect results, because a cached record may later change at the authoritative server. When name servers return resource records, each record carries a time-to-live field expressed in seconds, with 16 bits of significance. When a resolver caches a returned record it must remember the TTL and discard the record when that amount of time has passed. The model is that copies are distributed with timeouts for refreshing: the distributor sets the timeout value and the recipient of the distribution is responsible for performing the refresh.
sections.plainLanguage: The lookup program follows referrals from server to server until it reaches the one with the answer, and it keeps answers for a while so it does not have to ask again every time.
